name: Ravangla
tagline: A 130-foot Buddha, Pang Lhabsol and a ridge-top jeep junction
meta_description: Ravangla, South Sikkim: Buddha Park, Ralang monasteries, the Maenam hike and Pang Lhabsol, with shared-jeep fares, stays and 2026 costs.
summary: Ravangla is a ridge-top town at about 2,100 m between Pelling, Namchi and Gangtok. It is known for Buddha Park's 130-foot copper Buddha, consecrated by the Dalai Lama in 2013, and for Pang Lhabsol in late summer. Stay one or two nights to add Ralang, Temi and the Maenam hike.
intro: Ravangla, also spelt Rabong or Rabongla, is a ridge-top town at about 2,100 m on the road that links Pelling, Namchi and Gangtok. Wikipedia explains the name as Sikkimese: 'ra' for wild sheep, 'vong' for a rearing place and 'la' for a pass. The bazaar is small, a couple of streets of hotels, momo shops and jeep stands, and it fills with traffic around midday when jeeps from Gangtok and Gyalshing meet. On a clear morning Kangchenjunga, Pandim, Kabru and Siniolchu line up to the north.

Most people come for Buddha Park, or Tathagata Tsal, about 1 km from the bazaar. Its 130-foot (about 40 m) Buddha was built between 2006 and 2013 from some 60 tonnes of copper, to mark the 2,550th birth anniversary of the Buddha, and the 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it on 25 March 2013. Mount Narsing stands behind it. The statue sits in the grounds of the older Rabong Gompa, and its base holds a museum with a spiral gallery. Go early, before the day-trip cars arrive.

We like Ravangla as a one- or two-night base for the south rather than a quick photo stop. Ralang's two monasteries are about 6 km away, Temi Tea Garden ≈ 16–20 km, Namchi ≈ 27 km and Pelling ≈ 50 km. The Maenam ridge rises behind town for a full-day hike, and the Kunphenling Tibetan settlement, set up in 1978, sits on the slope above. Rooms usually cost less than in Pelling or Gangtok for the same comfort, and shared jeeps reach most of South and West Sikkim.

story.title: The mountain that witnessed an oath
paras: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, usually late August or September, and it is a festival that belongs to Sikkim alone. It honours Kangchenjunga as the guardian deity of the land. It also recalls a much older story. Sikkimese tradition holds that in the 13th century a Tibetan prince, Khye Bumsa, travelled to meet the Lepcha elder Thekong Tek because he and his wife had no children. The elder gave his blessing, and three sons followed.

The friendship that grew from that meeting was sealed as a blood-brotherhood at Kabi Longtsok, in today's North Sikkim. As the story is told, stone pillars were raised, animals were sacrificed and the mountain was called on as witness. From Khye Bumsa's line came Phuntsog Namgyal, crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom in 1642. So when Pang Lhabsol honours Kangchenjunga, it also marks the day Lepcha and Bhutia families promised to stand together, with the snow peak as their witness.

Ravangla now hosts a week-long Pang Lhabsol celebration with dances, cultural programmes and a fair; the 42nd edition ran from 30 August to 7 September 2025. Ralang Monastery nearby holds its own Pang Lhabsol rites and masked dances. Since 2013 the town has had a second landmark facing the same mountains: the copper Buddha of Tathagata Tsal. Festival dates follow the lunar calendar and move each year, so check current status before you travel.
story.source: Wikipedia: 'Khye Bumsa', 'Ralang Monastery', 'Buddha Park of Ravangla'; Sikkim government notices on the 2025 Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla

did_you_know: Ravangla's 130-foot Buddha was made from about 60 tonnes of copper using the repoussé technique, in which metal sheets are hammered into shape from the reverse side.
Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary, on the ridge above Ravangla, was set up in 1987 and covers about 36 sq km of forest known for medicinal plants.
The new Ralang Monastery, Palchen Choeling, was completed in 1995 under the 12th Gyaltsab Rinpoche of the Kagyu school, and the older Karma Rabtenling stands just to its west.
facts: Buddha Park, Ralang, Pang Lhabsol, Maenam hike

highlights.title: Buddha Park at opening time
highlights.text: The 130-foot copper Buddha of Tathagata Tsal faces the snow range with Mount Narsing behind. Walk the 1 km from the bazaar at opening time, when the light is soft and the car park is empty, then visit the museum in the base and the old Rabong Gompa next door.

highlights.title: Ralang's new and old monasteries
highlights.text: About 6 km from town, the large Palchen Choeling monastic institute of the Kagyu school was completed in 1995, and the older Karma Rabtenling sits just west of it. Go in the morning to hear prayers, and ask about masked dance days in the autumn.

highlights.title: Maenam ridge and Bhaleydhunga
highlights.text: The forested ridge behind Ravangla is the Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary, set up in 1987. A full-day hike of roughly 12 km each way climbs about 1,000 m towards the summit and the Bhaleydhunga rock face. Go with a local guide and register with the forest office first.

highlights.title: Kunphenling Tibetan settlement
highlights.text: Above the bazaar, the Kunphenling Tibetan settlement was set up in 1978. Walk up through prayer flags and small chortens to the carpet centre, where wool carpets are woven on upright looms. It is a quiet hour, and a good place to buy something that supports the families who make it.

highlights.title: Pang Lhabsol week
highlights.text: In late August or September Ravangla hosts Sikkim's main Pang Lhabsol celebration, honouring Kangchenjunga and the old Lepcha–Bhutia oath. Expect dances, cultural shows and a fair. It falls in the monsoon, so plan for rain and road delays and check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: A cheap base for the south
highlights.text: From Ravangla, shared jeeps run to Namchi for about ₹80–120 a seat and to Gangtok and Gyalshing every morning, indicative, 2026. Temi, Ralang and Namchi all fit into day trips, so you can unpack once and see most of South Sikkim.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from the Siliguri stands to Ravangla for about ₹350–450 a seat and from Gangtok for ₹250–350, indicative, 2026. Ravangla to Namchi costs about ₹80–120. For Pelling, take a jeep or bus to Gyalshing and change there for the short hop. Most departures are in the morning and afternoon seats are scarce, so start early and check current status before you travel.

A small car or SUV from Siliguri, NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹4,500–6,000 one way, indicative, 2026, for ≈ 120 km and 4.5–5 hours. From Gangtok the drive is ≈ 65 km and about 2.5–3 hours; from Pelling it is ≈ 50 km and 2–2.5 hours via Legship and Kewzing.
New Jalpaiguri (NJP) is the nearest major station, ≈ 120 km away. From NJP, take an auto to the Siliguri jeep stands for a shared seat, or book a car at the station for the 4.5–5 hour drive.

Bagdogra (IXB) is ≈ 130 km away and has the most flights. Pakyong airport near Gangtok is closer on the map, but its flights have been irregular, so check current status before you travel and plan around Bagdogra.

where_to_stay: Ravangla has a small spread of family-run hotels in the bazaar and along Kewzing Road, which leads out towards Pelling. Hotel Zumthang and Chingthang Hotel on Kewzing Road are simple budget options within walking distance of the jeep stand. For more space and a view, Mt. Narsing Village Resort sits about 4 km out on the Gangtok–Pelling road, with a cheaper roadside wing and an upper annexe of cottages facing Narsing and Kabru. Village homestays around Ravangla and Ralang cost less again and include home-cooked meals. Book ahead for Pang Lhabsol week and the October holidays; rates are usually lower in winter and the monsoon.
budget_tip: Walk the 1 km from the bazaar to Buddha Park instead of paying for a taxi, and use the morning shared jeep to Namchi at about ₹80–120 a seat rather than a reserved car.
tips: Reach Buddha Park at opening time for clear views and an empty courtyard; by late morning cloud often hides the peaks.
Nights are cold for much of the year at 2,100 m, so carry a warm layer even in April and October.
Snow sometimes falls on the upper slopes in January and February; roads usually clear within a day, but check current status before you travel.
Buy onward jeep tickets the evening before at the stand, as morning seats to Gangtok and Siliguri fill first.
Dress modestly and walk clockwise around the statue and the chortens, as local visitors do.

experiences.title: Buddha Park and Rabong Gompa at first light
experiences.summary: Walk 1 km from the bazaar to Tathagata Tsal, where a 130-foot copper Buddha faces the snow range with Mount Narsing behind. Add the museum in the statue's base and the older Rabong Gompa in the same grounds, ideally before the day-trip crowds arrive.
body: Buddha Park, also called Tathagata Tsal, lies about 1 km from Ravangla's bazaar, an easy walk on a quiet road. The statue is 130 feet (about 40 m) high and was made from roughly 60 tonnes of copper using the repoussé method. Work ran from 2006 to 2013, for the 2,550th birth anniversary of the Buddha, and the 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it on 25 March 2013. On a clear day Mount Narsing and the Kangchenjunga range sit behind it.

Inside the base there is a museum with a spiral gallery that tells the Buddha's life in paintings and models. Walk it slowly, clockwise, the way pilgrims do. The park also has a meditation centre and a small lake, Cho Djo, ringed by forest. The grounds belong to the older Rabong Gompa, a pilgrimage site long before the statue, and it is worth stepping into its prayer hall before you leave.

Entry is about ₹50–100 per person, indicative, 2026, so check current status before you travel. Come at opening time: the light is softer, the courtyard is empty and the peaks are more likely to be clear. By late morning cars from Gangtok and Namchi arrive and cloud often builds. There is little shade on the main terrace, so carry water and a hat in spring. Shoes come off inside the gompa and the museum, so wear a pair that slips on and off easily.

faqs.q: How tall is the Buddha statue at Ravangla
faqs.a: The Buddha at Ravangla's Buddha Park is 130 feet, about 40 m, tall. It was built between 2006 and 2013 from about 60 tonnes of copper to mark the 2,550th birth anniversary of the Buddha. The 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it on 25 March 2013. Mount Narsing forms the backdrop on a clear day.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Buddha Park Ravangla
faqs.a: Expect to pay about ₹50–100 per person, indicative for 2026. Fees and camera charges can change, so check current status before you travel. The park is about 1 km from the bazaar, so most people walk rather than take a taxi. Allow two to three hours for the statue, museum and Rabong Gompa together.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to visit Buddha Park
faqs.a: Go at opening time in the morning. The light is soft, the courtyard is quiet and Kangchenjunga and Narsing are most often clear before 10 am, especially from October to December. By late morning day-trip cars arrive from Gangtok and Namchi and clouds tend to build over the ridge.

experiences.title: Ralang's new and old monasteries
experiences.best_time: Mornings; autumn for masked dance days
experiences.cost: Free entry; taxi from Ravangla ₹800–1,500 return, indicative
experiences.summary: A short drive from Ravangla, Ralang has two Kagyu monasteries side by side: the large Palchen Choeling, completed in 1995, and the older Karma Rabtenling just west of it. Come for morning prayers, wall paintings and thangkas, and ask about masked dance dates.
body: Ralang Monastery sits about 6 km from Ravangla and belongs to the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism. The new complex, formally the Palchen Choeling Monastic Institute, was completed in 1995 under the 12th Gyaltsab Rinpoche and follows traditional Tibetan design. It is large, with a wide courtyard where young monks study and play, and a main hall known for its collection of paintings and thangkas. Most visitors come by taxi from Ravangla and ask the driver to wait while they walk between the two buildings.

Just west stands the older Karma Rabtenling monastery, smaller and quieter, which was rebuilt between 1975 and 1981. Walk between the two to see how much has changed in a few decades: one is a working village gompa, the other a monastic teaching institute on a much larger scale. Ralang's calendar is full: Wikipedia lists Pang Lhabsol rites honouring Kangchenjunga, masked chaam dances in the 7th and 10th Tibetan months, a Mahakala festival and the Kagyed ritual that runs into early December.

Entry is free; leave a small offering if you wish. A taxi from Ravangla costs about ₹800–1,500 return with waiting, indicative, 2026, or ask at the stand for a shared jeep heading that way. Dress modestly, remove shoes and hats in the halls and ask before photographing monks or the inside of shrines. Dance dates follow the lunar calendar and draw large local crowds, so arrive early for a spot on the courtyard steps and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Ralang Monastery from Ravangla
faqs.a: Ralang Monastery is about 6 km from Ravangla by most accounts, a short drive downhill. A taxi with waiting costs roughly ₹800–1,500 return, indicative for 2026. Allow half a day to see both the new Palchen Choeling and the older Karma Rabtenling, and to sit in on morning prayers.

faqs.q: When are the masked dances at Ralang
faqs.a: Ralang holds chaam masked dances on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, around Pang Lhabsol in August or September, and on the 29th day of the 10th month, usually in November or December. The Kagyed ritual runs into early December. Lunar dates move every year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Ralang Monastery
faqs.a: Photography in the courtyards is usually fine, but always ask before shooting inside the prayer halls or photographing monks, and never use flash near paintings and thangkas. Rules differ by hall and by day, especially during rituals. A polite question to the caretaker monk at the door settles it.

experiences.title: Maenam ridge hike with a local guide
experiences.best_time: Apr–May for flowers; Oct–Nov for views
experiences.cost: Guide roughly ₹1,500–2,500 per group plus a small forest fee, indicative
experiences.summary: A long, steep day walk from Ravangla into Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary, climbing about 1,000 m over roughly 12 km to the ridge top and the Bhaleydhunga rock face. You need a local guide, forest registration, an early start and a clear day for the views.
body: Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary covers about 36 sq km of forest on the ridge behind Ravangla. It was set up in 1987, and its name is usually explained as a treasure house of medicines, after the medicinal plants that grow here. The trail starts near town and climbs steadily through oak, rhododendron and bamboo. Expect roughly 12 km and about 1,000 m of ascent to the top, which takes most fit walkers three to four hours.

Near the summit, the Bhaleydhunga rock face drops away to the south. On a clear morning you see across to the Kangchenjunga range and down to the Rangeet valley. Birders come for laughingthrushes, verditer flycatchers and, with luck, the satyr tragopan. A walking day here is mostly forest and mist, and that is part of the point. Carry lunch, water and a rain shell, because cloud builds fast after noon.

Do not go alone. Trails split and are poorly marked, and the forest is thick. Hire a local guide through your hotel; expect about ₹1,500–2,500 for a group, plus a small forest entry fee paid at the forest office, indicative, 2026. Register before you start. Leave by 6 am to be down before dark, and tell your hotel your plan and expected return time. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long is the Maenam trek from Ravangla
faqs.a: Plan a full day. The climb is roughly 12 km with about 1,000 m of ascent, and most fit walkers take three to four hours up and a little less down. With stops for lunch and views, eight to ten hours is realistic. Start by 6 am so you are off the ridge before the afternoon cloud and dark.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for Maenam
faqs.a: Yes, we strongly recommend one. The trail forks often, markings are poor and fog can close in quickly. A local guide also knows where to register and pay the forest fee. Your Ravangla hotel can arrange one for roughly ₹1,500–2,500 a group, indicative for 2026; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best season for the Maenam hike
faqs.a: April and May bring rhododendrons and orchids in the forest, though haze can blur distant views. October and November give the clearest mountain views and dry trails. Avoid June to September, when the path is slippery, leeches are common and views are usually lost in cloud. Winter is possible but cold on top.

experiences.title: Kunphenling settlement and Pang Lhabsol week
experiences.best_time: Any clear morning; Pang Lhabsol in Aug–Sep
experiences.summary: Walk up to the Kunphenling Tibetan settlement, set up in 1978, to see carpet weaving and village life above the bazaar. If your dates allow, time your stay for Pang Lhabsol, when Ravangla honours Kangchenjunga with a week of dances, cultural programmes and a fair.
body: The Kunphenling Tibetan settlement sits on the slope above Ravangla and was set up in 1978. Wikipedia counts a Tibetan community of about 1,300 people around Ravangla, with schools, monasteries and health centres. A slow walk up takes you past prayer flags, small chortens and kitchen gardens to the carpet centre, where weavers work wool on upright looms. You can watch for a while and buy direct, which helps the families who make them.

Pang Lhabsol is Sikkim's own festival, held on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month. It honours Kangchenjunga as the land's guardian deity and remembers, in Sikkimese tradition, the blood-brotherhood sworn between the Lepcha elder Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa with the mountain as witness. Ravangla hosts a week of dances, cultural shows and a fair; the 42nd edition ran from 30 August to 7 September 2025.

Both are free. The settlement is open to respectful visitors; ask before photographing people or homes. During festival week rooms fill early, so book well ahead and expect higher prices. It falls in the monsoon, which means rain, leeches on forest paths and possible landslides on the roads in. Pack a good rain jacket, leave a spare day at the end of your trip and keep cash, as card machines fail in bad weather. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol in Ravangla
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month, which lands in late August or September. Ravangla runs a week-long celebration around it; in 2025 the 42nd edition ran from 30 August to 7 September. The lunar date moves every year, so check current status before you travel and book rooms early.

faqs.q: What does Pang Lhabsol celebrate
faqs.a: It honours Kangchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity. In Sikkimese tradition it also recalls the blood-brotherhood sworn at Kabi Longtsok between the Lepcha elder Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa, with the mountain called on as witness. For many Sikkimese it is a festival of Lepcha and Bhutia unity.

faqs.q: Can visitors walk into the Tibetan settlement at Ravangla
faqs.a: Yes, respectful visitors are welcome to walk through Kunphenling and visit the carpet centre. Keep to paths, do not enter homes or monastery rooms uninvited and ask before taking photos of people. Buying a carpet or small woven piece directly is a good way to support the community. There is no entry fee.

faqs.q: Is Ravangla worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for one or two nights. Ravangla has Buddha Park's 130-foot Buddha, Ralang's two monasteries 6 km away, the Maenam ridge hike and wide views of Kangchenjunga on clear mornings. It also costs less than Pelling or Gangtok and works as a base for Temi Tea Garden and Namchi. Skip it only if you are very short of time.

faqs.q: How far is Ravangla from Gangtok and Pelling
faqs.a: Ravangla is ≈ 65 km from Gangtok, about 2.5–3 hours by road, and ≈ 50 km from Pelling, about 2–2.5 hours via Legship and Kewzing. Namchi is ≈ 27 km away, about an hour. Shared jeeps run on all three roads, mostly in the morning, so plan transfers early in the day.

faqs.q: How do I reach Ravangla from NJP by shared jeep
faqs.a: Go from NJP or Bagdogra to the Siliguri jeep stands and take a shared jeep to Ravangla for about ₹350–450 a seat, indicative for 2026. The ≈ 120 km ride takes 4.5–5 hours. Jeeps leave in the morning, so arrive early. If you miss them, take a jeep to Namchi and change. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ravangla
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest mountain views and dry roads. March to May brings rhododendrons and orchids, with some afternoon haze. January and February are cold but clear, with occasional snow on the upper slopes. June to September is monsoon: cheaper rooms but frequent cloud and landslide delays, though Pang Lhabsol falls then.

faqs.q: Does it snow in Ravangla
faqs.a: Sometimes. Snow falls on the higher slopes around Ravangla in some winters, mostly in January and February. Snow is not reliable, so do not plan a trip around it, and it rarely lasts long when it comes. Roads can close briefly after heavy snow, so check current status before you travel and carry proper warm clothing.

faqs.q: Do foreigners need a permit for Ravangla
faqs.a: Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, which is free and valid for 30 days. Apply online through e-FRRO or get it at the Melli or Rangpo checkposts on the way in. Indian nationals need no permit for Ravangla but should carry photo ID. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do you need in Ravangla
faqs.a: One full day covers Buddha Park, Rabong Gompa, Ralang and the Tibetan settlement. Two nights let you add Temi Tea Garden or a day trip to Namchi without rushing. Add a third night only if you plan the full-day Maenam hike, which needs an early start and a clear day.

faqs.q: Is Ravangla good for families with children and seniors
faqs.a: Yes. Buddha Park is a short, mostly level walk from the bazaar, and the statue, museum and gardens hold children's interest. Ralang and Temi are easy drives. Seniors should note the cold nights at 2,100 m and the steep lanes around the bazaar. Skip the Maenam hike unless everyone is fit.

faqs.q: How much does a trip to Ravangla cost
faqs.a: On a budget, two nights in Ravangla cost roughly ₹4,000–7,000 per person, using shared jeeps from Siliguri, a simple hotel on Kewzing Road and local meals at ₹150–350, indicative for 2026. A reserved car from Siliguri adds ₹4,500–6,000 each way. Mid-range resorts and festival week raise the total.
